scope_summary: Prime coat application for bare drywall CEILINGS in new construction. Single prime coat over new drywall. Assumes drywall is taped, mudded, and sanded by drywall contractor. NO edge work required — ceiling primer can overlap onto wall area because walls will be primed/painted after. Companion spec to SF_DRYWALL_CEILINGS_NC_PAINT (finish coats).
relevant_findings: NC production sequence: Prime ceilings → Prime walls → Paint ceilings → Paint walls. Ceiling primer goes first.
NO edge work at ceiling-wall boundary — walls haven't been primed yet. Ceiling primer can overlap 1-2 inches onto wall area.
PVA primer is the standard for NC drywall ceilings — economical, seals porous drywall, excellent base for ceiling paint
Acrylic latex primer for QT4+ provides superior adhesion and topcoat holdout
High-build primer may be needed for Level 5 drywall finish or when uniform porosity is critical (QT5)
Spray+backroll is production standard for ceiling priming in NC — best coverage and speed balance
Overhead work is approximately 15-20% slower than equivalent wall priming
Single primer coat is standard — drywall absorbs primer uniformly when properly prepared
Drywall fasteners in new construction are covered with mud and are rust-resistant — NO spot-priming of fasteners is needed
Drywall dust on ceilings is the primary contamination concern — must be removed before priming

Recessed lighting locations and ceiling electrical box locations require protection from overspray (spray methods). In NC, these are often OPEN HOLES where fixtures have not yet been installed — they still must be filled with paper to prevent overspray entry and to keep blown-in/blown-out insulation from coming through during spraying.
Window/door masking for spray methods is lightweight — pin plastic up over openings to prevent fallout, not intricate masking
At this NC phase, typically only exterior doors are installed (sliders, front entry, back entry, garage entry). Interior doors are usually not installed yet, though this is not always the case.
Floor condition varies — may be subfloor only, or tile/finished floors may already be installed in bathrooms or other areas. Specs must account for both conditions.
Primer application is a binary task — properly sealed or not. Quality tier affects scrutiny of inspection, not primer application technique.

Sanding primed surface before finish coat is a finish task step — it belongs in the finish spec (SF_DRYWALL_CEILINGS_NC_PAINT), not the prime spec. QT4+ finish specs include sanding before first finish coat.

clarifications_from_field.rationale: New construction drywall fasteners are covered with mud and are rust-resistant. There is no need to spot-prime fasteners on new drywall. This is a common misconception.
Walls have NOT been primed or painted yet. Ceiling primer can overlap onto wall area. Wall primer covers this when applied.
While NC often has subfloor only, finished floors (tile in bathrooms, hardwood, etc.) may already be installed before prime phase. Floor protection must be conditionally included based on floor_type.

At this phase, just pinning plastic up over openings to prevent overspray fallout. Not intricate masking. Typically the FIRST masking in NC sequence. Only exterior doors are usually installed at this point (interior doors typically not yet hung).
This is prime-only. Finish coats handled by companion spec SF_DRYWALL_CEILINGS_NC_PAINT.
Dry time depends heavily on humidity, ventilation, temperature, and how masked off the space is. Do not pin down specific dry times in specs — too many variables.

prep_requirements.method: HEPA vacuum with brush attachment on ceiling surface
prep_requirements.reason: Drywall dust on ceilings reduces adhesion and causes visible contamination in primer film

prep_requirements.method: Walk with work light, mark defects on ceiling
prep_requirements.reason: Identify unfilled joints, damaged paper before priming
prep_requirements.skip_conditions: QT2 may reduce to major defects only

limitations: Seals porosity only — does not block stains, tannins, or discoloration
typical_products: Benjamin Moore Ultra Spec PVA Primer
PVA_primer.notes: PVA primer is a drywall sealer only. It has no stain blocking properties whatsoever. Do not confuse with shellac-based or stain-blocking primers — they serve entirely different purposes.

limitations: Longer dry time than PVA (varies by conditions)
acrylic_latex_primer.notes: Acrylic latex drywall primer provides better adhesion and holdout than PVA but does NOT provide stain blocking. For stain blocking, a dedicated stain-blocking primer is a separate product category.

typical_products: Benjamin Moore Ultra Spec High Build Primer
high_build_primer.notes: High-build is for surface uniformity, not stain blocking.

drywall_finish_level_impacts.description: Tape embedded in joint compound, two coats on joints and one on fasteners
drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Higher absorption on ceiling, may show joint pattern through single prime coat
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Acceptable for utility areas, may need second prime for visible ceilings

drywall_finish_level_impacts.description: Level 3 plus additional skim coat on joints and fasteners
drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Standard absorption, single prime coat typically sufficient
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Most common in residential and commercial NC

drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Uniform surface, good primer holdout, may require light sand after prime
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Required for high sheen ceiling finishes, critical lighting conditions

common_failure_modes.cause: Different absorption rates between joint compound and paper face on ceiling
common_failure_modes.prevention: Use high-build primer for Level 3 drywall, consider double prime
common_failure_modes.remediation: Additional primer coat, consider high-build product

common_failure_modes.cause: Drywall dust contamination — especially problematic on ceilings where dust settles
Insufficient inspection, overhead angle makes holidays harder to see
common_failure_modes.prevention: Work with adequate lighting, overlap passes, backroll for spray methods

common_failure_modes.cause: Overhead application causes primer to sag before drying — worse on ceilings than walls
common_failure_modes.prevention: Proper mil thickness, don't overload roller/spray tip
common_failure_modes.remediation: Sand drips flat, reprime affected area

required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Always — primary quantity driver for ceiling priming

required_paintscope_keys.description: Room count for ceiling fixture protection heuristic
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Spray methods require ceiling fixture protection

required_paintscope_keys.description: Count of window openings to mask for overspray fallout protection
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Spray methods — lightweight plastic pinned over openings to prevent fallout

required_paintscope_keys.description: Count of door openings to mask for overspray fallout protection. At this NC phase, typically exterior doors only (sliders, entry doors, garage entry).
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Spray methods — lightweight plastic pinned over openings to prevent fallout

proposed_new_keys.description: Floor area requiring vacuum cleanup after overhead work (priming, painting ceilings). Distinct from floor protection keys — this drives cleanup labor, not material protection.
proposed_new_keys.justification: PS_PROTECT_SF.FLOOR_EXPOSED is semantically wrong for vacuum tasks. Vacuuming is cleanup, not protection. A dedicated key avoids conflating protection setup with post-work cleanup.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: NO edge work — walls not yet primed or painted. Ceiling primer can overlap onto wall area.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Wall primer covers ceiling overlap when applied. No edge work task needed.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: NOT applicable — trim not installed (pre-trim phase)
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Crown molding installed and painted separately after walls

zones.notes: Stuff recessed cans and ceiling electrical boxes with paper, tape over face. Required for spray methods. Not needed for roll-only.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Activates ONLY when finished floors are present. Subfloor-only conditions skip floor protection entirely.
zones.notes: Tile in bathrooms, hardwood, or other finished flooring may already be installed before prime phase. Floor protection required when present.

protection_zones_analysis.method_notes: Roll method: fixture_covers NOT required (no overspray). Spray+backroll: fixture_covers REQUIRED. Window/door masking is lightweight — pin plastic over openings, not intricate masking.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: No edge work needed — walls not yet primed. Ceiling primer overlaps onto wall area. Wall primer covers overlap.

affected_conditions.notes: Floor protection tasks activate ONLY when finished floors are present. NC may have tile, hardwood, or other finished floors installed before prime phase. Do not assume subfloor-only.

values.definition: Unfinished subfloor — no protection needed for floor surface
Finished flooring installed (tile, hardwood, LVP, carpet, etc.) — floor protection required
Mixed — some areas finished, some subfloor. Per-room floor protection decisions.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: cold_below_50f=1.30x (extended dry), hot_above_90f=1.15x (reduced open time) per Modifier_Registry
affected_conditions.notes: Temperature affects primer dry time and open time. Cold conditions may prevent proper film formation. NC buildings may lack HVAC during prime phase.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: No modifier values defined yet (placeholder condition in vocabulary)
affected_conditions.notes: NC interiors may have limited ventilation before HVAC install. Affects dry times significantly — especially with masked-off spaces reducing airflow.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: See height modifiers H1-H4 in Modifier_Registry. Ceiling work inherently requires overhead access.
affected_conditions.notes: Standard 8-10ft ceilings: floor-level or step ladder. Higher ceilings require extension ladder or scaffold. Ceiling priming amplifies height impact due to overhead angle.

not_applicable_conditions.reason: New construction — always vacant during prime phase
New construction — no existing paint. Lead not applicable.
New drywall should be dry. If active moisture, stop work — not a modifier, it's a hold.
NC production schedule is standard. Accelerated/phased not typical for prime phase.

recessed_lights_per_room.notes: Recessed cans per room in ceiling

ceiling_electrical_boxes_per_room.notes: Junction boxes, smoke detector locations, fan boxes per room

original_research.claim: Spot-priming ceiling fasteners is critical to prevent rust bleed-through on finish coats

research_corrections.corrected_value: New construction drywall fasteners are covered with mud and are rust-resistant. No spot-priming of fasteners is needed.
research_corrections.rationale: Field correction from contractor. Fasteners in new drywall are mudded over by the drywall contractor and use rust-resistant screws. Spot-priming is not required and wastes labor.

original_research.claim: PVA primer has 'less stain blocking than shellac' and acrylic latex has 'better stain blocking'

research_corrections.corrected_value: PVA and acrylic latex drywall primers have ZERO stain blocking capability. They are sealers only. Stain-blocking primers are an entirely separate product category. Do not rely on marketing claims.
research_corrections.rationale: Field correction from contractor. Marketing materials misleadingly suggest drywall primers have stain blocking properties. They do not. Shellac-based stain blockers and PVA sealers serve completely different purposes.

research_corrections.rationale: Field correction from contractor. Not all NC projects have subfloor-only conditions at prime phase. Specs must be all-inclusive.

research_corrections.corrected_value: Do not specify primer dry times. Dry time depends on humidity, ventilation, temperature, and how masked off the space is. Too many variables to pin down.
